answers.justification: C6 shows tenured agents' FCR fell just as far (75.1→67.3 and 75.0→67.2) as the April intake's 66.4%, and billing referral rates were similar by tenure (56/54/53%). C1 and C3 show a normal cohort, so the intake does not explain the site fall.

FC-0417 cut the in-call credit limit from £100 to £25 and auto-opens BRT referrals (C11). Billing referrals jumped from 7% to 54% in w/c 14 Apr (C6), while referred FCR (~33%) and non-referred FCR (82%) stayed flat. That shift in billing calls alone takes billing FCR from 79% to 56% and accounts for the whole ~8-point site drop, since other contact reasons were unchanged (C6, E2).

The IVR went live on 28 Apr, after FCR had already fallen in w/c 14 and 21 Apr (E2, E3). The misrouting proxy did not worsen (3.8% vs 4.0%, C2), and FCR within non-billing contact reasons did not move (C6).

Occupancy and handle time rose only modestly (C4), but FCR held steady for payments, moving home, meter calls and non-referred billing calls (C6). A centre-wide workload effect would have lowered those too, so the extra workload looks like a result of repeat contacts rather than a cause.

Tariff calls doubled their share (6%→12%), but they have high FCR (86→85%, C6), so that mix shift would push site FCR up, not down. FCR was also flat in the first two weeks after the 1 April increase (E2: 75.1%, 74.8%).

FC-0417 makes the system block adjustments over £25 and automatically open a BRT referral (C11). Referrals stepped up exactly in w/c 14 Apr (C6), equally across tenure bands, which rules out the intake as the rival explanation, and BRT says much of the new work is small adjustments (C8).

Referred billing calls resolve at ~33% against a stable 82% for non-referred calls (C6), and 58% of sampled repeat contacts after a referral were chasing its status (C6). The rise in referrals arithmetically accounts for the whole site drop, while every other reason's FCR stayed flat.

The intake's FCR (66.4%) is barely different from tenured agents (67.2–67.3%), and the tenured bands fell by the same 8 points (C6). The shared start date of 14 Apr (E3) is a coincidence, not a cause.

Complaints rose from 41 to 47–50 per 10,000 at the same time as the FCR drop (E5). However, complaints are not linked to the originating call and 64% are uncategorised (E5), so causation cannot be established.

A1 targets the cause identified in C6/C11 and meets the financial controller's stated condition (a compensating control proven on a limited population, C11). The limit is a one-day configuration change, and MI can track the trial teams within a day (C6).

The intake agents perform like tenured agents (C6), so putting them on performance plans would punish the wrong group (E6) and leave the referral cause untouched; with site FCR around 67%, many agents across all tenures would fall below the 65% cut-off.

A3 may well be the right end state, but Finance requires post-call sampling to be shown on a limited population to keep unsupported credits below 1% first (C11, IA-11 £41,200 finding), and that is not yet established.

Better visibility of contact reason and referral status is reasonable given the dashboard's blind spots (E2), but MI can already rerun the breakdown within a day (C6). That makes three months of analyst time a lower priority than fixing the credit limit.
C6's decomposition by contact reason, referral status and tenure, together with C11's mechanism and timing, is enough to commit to the limited, monitored trial in A1.

ambiguousItems: S12: premature vs harmful — rolling out everywhere at once goes ahead of Finance's evidence condition on a protective audit control (C11), but it is backed by sampling, so 'harmful' is arguable rather than clear.
S13: acceptable vs premature — the item depends on no hypothesis, but its cost and the fact that a one-day MI rerun already exists (C6) could push it lower.
S07: causal vs association-only — the evidence is observational, but the stratification and the C6 repeat-contact sample make a causal reading strong.
S09: association-only vs causal — the timing and the 'Service – delay' category hint at a mechanism, but complaints are not linked to the originating call.
caseProblems: C6 settles almost the whole case in one item: the decomposition by reason, referral and tenure answers H1–H5 and R1–R3 together. That makes the case easy once C6 is collected, and its title ('by contact reason, referral status and agent tenure') signals how useful it is.
C11's financial controller's note (30 Jul) almost word-for-word describes A1 (a compensating control on a limited population), which leaks the preferred action.

Minor inconsistency: C8 says BRT turnaround roughly doubled (3 → 6–7 working days) and two staff are on long-term sick (C5), yet C6 reports referred-call FCR unchanged or slightly better (33% → 34%) under a 7-day window. A longer backlog would be expected to lower referred FCR.
C6 figures reconcile exactly (billing 0.07×33+0.93×82≈79; 0.54×34+0.46×82≈56; site ≈75.0 → 67.1), which is good internal consistency but rather tidy for real MI data.

rulings.explanation: A3 fits the 'premature' definition closely. It would be the right move if post-call sampling keeps unsupported credits below 1%, which is exactly the controller's untested condition in C11. 'Harmful' is a weaker fit. A3 does not remove the audit control: it swaps the hard £25 block for a compensating sampling control. It punishes no one and hides no information. C11 also says the limit is a one-working-day configuration change, so a wrong call can be reversed quickly. The worst case is a return toward the Q4 rate of unsupported credits (3.4%, about £41k a quarter) until the change is reversed. That loss is limited and reversible, not likely lasting harm. Going ahead of Finance's evidence condition makes the action unjustified now, which is what 'premature' means. It does not make the action likely to worsen outcomes.
rulings.fix: No change needed. Optional hardening: add 'and without Finance sign-off' to the A3 wording only if the authors want 'harmful'. As written, 'premature' is the single best answer.

rulings.explanation: 'Premature' needs the action to depend on a hypothesis that is not yet confirmed. A4 (a permanent reason- and referral-level dashboard) depends on none. It is useful whichever cause is true. So the only real alternatives are 'preferred' and 'acceptable'. The revised A4 text gives a real cost: about three months of an analyst's time, deferring other MI reports. C6 says MI can rerun the same breakdown for any set of teams within a day, which covers tracking the A1 trial. So A4 is sensible but adds nothing the next decision needs. That rules out 'preferred' and leaves 'acceptable'. Nothing in the evidence makes A4 harmful.

The evidence for R2 is close to a natural experiment. C11 shows the jump in referral share came from an outside system rule change, not from any change in the calls or the agents. C6 shows FCR within each stratum stayed the same: referred calls about 33–34%, non-referred 82%. The shift in mix alone reproduces the billing fall (79% to 56%) and the whole site fall. FCR for other contact reasons is flat, and the tenure data rule out the intake rival. The main confounder would be that referred calls are simply harder cases. That is answered because the newly forced referrals (previously settled in-call) did not raise referred-call FCR. C6's repeat-contact sample also gives the mechanism: 58% of repeat contacts after a referral were customers chasing referral status or a promised callback. Temporal order, mechanism, covariation and a ruled-out main rival together meet the definition of 'causal'. 'Association-only' would ignore the outside forcing and the stratified decomposition.

E2 and E5 show complaints rising (41 to 47–50 per 10,000 contacts) in the same months FCR fell, so there is an association. But the 1 April tariff increase is a rival with the same timing, and 'Price/tariff' is the largest categorised complaint group. 64% of complaints are uncategorised, and complaints are counted by month received, not linked to the originating call. Monthly data cannot separate a 1 April cause from a 14 April cause. The 24% 'Service – delay' share hints at a mechanism but does not rule out the rival. No catalogue item settles it: C10 is site-level only and dropped the repeat-contact question. So 'causal' is not established, and the co-movement is enough to rule out 'unknown'. 'Association-only' is the only defensible answer.
